item.title: Go Daily Question 20250601
item.description:
What is the output of the following code?

var p *int

func foo() (*int, error) {
 var i int = 5
 return &i, nil
}

func bar() {
 //use p
 fmt.Println(*p)
}

func main() {
 p, err := foo()
 if err != nil {
 fmt.Println(err)
 return
 }
 bar()
 fmt.Println(*p)
}

A. 5 5 B. runtime error

🔑 Answer Analysis:

B The global *p is nil. In p, err := foo(), p here is a new local variable and is unrelated to the global p.

item.title: Go Daily Question 20250509
item.description:
Usually, closure questions are a must-have in JS interviews. With more and more languages supporting the functional paradigm, closure problems frequently appear. The same is true in Go.

This is a problem from Go Language Enthusiasts Weekly #90. What is the output of the following code?

package main

import "fmt"

func app() func(string) string {
	t := "Hi"
	c := func(b string) string {
		t = t + " " + b
		return t
	}
	return c
}

func main() {
	a := app()
	b := app()
	a("go")
	fmt.Println(b("All"))
	fmt.Println(a("All"))
}
🔑 Answer Analysis:

Closure fmt.Println(b("All")) outputs A (Hi All) fmt.Println(a("All")) outputs B (Hi go All)

item.title: Go Daily Question 145
item.description:
To define a package-level global string variable, which of the following syntax is correct (multiple choice):

  • A. var str string
  • B. str := ""
  • C. str = ""
  • D. var str = ""
🔑 Answer Analysis:

A, D

Only var can be used for global definitions.

B: Only supports local variable declaration. C: Assignment, not definition.

item.title: Go Daily Question 120
item.description:
In the following code, x is declared, y is not declared. Determine whether each statement is correct.

A: x, _ := f()
B: x, _ = f()
C: x, y := f()
D: x, y = f()
🔑 Answer Analysis:

A is wrong, B is correct, C is correct, D is wrong.

item.title: Go Daily Question 085
item.description:
Which of the following options is correct?

func main() {
 if a := 1; false {
 } else if b := 2; false {
 } else {
 println(a, b)
 }
}

A. 1 2 B. compilation error

🔑 Answer Analysis:

Involves code block issues. For details, you can refer to this article: https://studygolang.com/articles/35587 After expanding, the code becomes:

{
 a := 1
 if false {

 } else {
 b := 2
 if false {

 } else {
 println(a, b)
 }
 }
 }

item.title: Go Daily Question 074
item.description:
What is the output of the following code?

package main

import "fmt"

func app() func(string) string {
 t := "Hi"
 c := func(b string) string {
 t = t + " " + b
 return t
 }
 return c
}

func main() {
 a := app()
 b := app()
 a("go")
 fmt.Println(b("All"))
 fmt.Println(a("All"))
}

A: Hi All; B: Hi go All; C: Hi; D: go Al

🔑 Answer Analysis:

Closure fmt.Println(b("All")) outputs A (Hi All) fmt.Println(a("All")) outputs B (Hi go All)

item.title: Go Daily Question 053
item.description:
To define a package-level global string variable, which of the following syntax is correct (multiple choice):

A. var str string B. str := "" C. str = "" D. var str = ""

🔑 Answer Analysis:

A, D The key is “package-level global”. B: := can only be used inside functions. C: This is an assignment, not a declaration.

item.title: Go Daily Question 022
item.description:
Will the following code compile? If so, what will be the output?

package main

var(
 size := 1024
 max_size = size*2
)

func main() {
 fmt.Println(size,max_size)
}
🔑 Answer Analysis:

Answer: No.

var(
 size := 1024
)
Does not conform to specification.
Problem 1: `var` variable declaration cannot use `:=`.
Problem 2: `:=` can only be used inside a function; this problem uses it for declaring global variables.

Reference Analysis: The main point of this problem is the short variable declaration mode, such as: x := 100.
